title: Leader election, split-brain and fencing
problem: A leader pauses for a long garbage collection, its lease expires and a new leader is elected, then the old one wakes and keeps writing as if nothing happened.
summary: Leader election rents leadership with a lease: hold a time-limited key, renew it, and let the next candidate take over when it lapses. A paused leader cannot know its lease expired, so the storage it writes to checks a fencing token and rejects it.
catTip: I was the only cat allowed on the warm laptop, then I dozed off on the stairs. When I came back another cat had the lease and the laptop lid, sensibly, checked whose turn it was. Fencing, not feelings.

recall.q: A leader holding a 15-second lease stops for a 30-second GC pause. Walk through what happens and what stops the damage.
recall.a: The coordination service expires the lease and elects a new leader while the old one is frozen; when it resumes it still believes it leads and sends its pending writes, so two leaders act at once (split-brain). A fencing token, a number that increases with every new leader, lets the storage reject the old leader's writes because they carry a lower token than the one it has already seen.

guide.breaks: Two processes that both believe they are the leader run the same job twice, write conflicting data or send duplicate payments, and the lease that was meant to prevent it cannot wake a paused process to tell it that it lost.
guide.tradeoffs: A short lease detects a dead leader quickly but causes needless failovers on every slow heartbeat, a long one leaves the job unattended, and fencing only works if every system the leader writes to is changed to check the token.
guide.explainSimply: Think of a library with one key to the archive, lent out for an hour at a time. If the borrower falls asleep and the key is reissued to someone else, the sleeper wakes up still believing the archive is theirs. The fix is a door that checks the latest key number instead of trusting whoever is holding a key.
guide.hint: Ask who can still tell the paused leader that it has lost, and notice that it is not the lease; it has to be whatever receives the writes.

meow: My lease on the laptop lapsed mid-nap. The lid asked for my token, saw an old number, and said no. Fenced, not offended.

quiz.prompt: A leader renews a 15-second lease every 5 seconds, then freezes in a 40-second stop-the-world GC pause. Which statement is true when it resumes?
options: It is still the leader, because a lease is only released by an explicit resign
It immediately knows it lost leadership, because the coordination service notified it during the pause
It may issue writes believing it still leads until something downstream rejects them; a fencing token makes the storage do that
Garbage collection pauses cannot outlast a lease, so the scenario cannot happen
quiz.explanation: Nothing in the process runs during the pause, so no notification is handled and its first action on resuming may be a stale write; only a check at the receiving side, such as a fencing token, stops it. Pauses longer than a lease are rare but real, which is the whole problem.

quiz.prompt: Which of these works as a fencing token?
options: A random UUID generated by each new leader
A number that increases with every leadership change, such as a ZooKeeper zxid, checked by the storage against the highest it has seen
The leader's wall-clock time at the moment of election
quiz.explanation: Fencing needs an order the storage can compare, so the token must increase with every new leader and the storage must remember the highest it has accepted. A UUID identifies a leader but cannot be ordered, and wall clocks on different machines can disagree in either direction.

cards.q: How does the classic ZooKeeper leader-election recipe work, and why does each client watch its predecessor rather than the leader?
cards.a: Each candidate creates an ephemeral sequential znode under an election path; the lowest sequence number is the leader, and the znode vanishes when its session expires. Watching only the next-lower znode means a leader failure wakes one client rather than all of them, avoiding the herd effect.

cards.q: When would you pick single-leader, multi-leader or leaderless replication?
cards.a: Single-leader when you need one clear write order and can tolerate a short failover (SQL primaries, Raft groups, Kafka partitions). Multi-leader when writes must be accepted in several regions or offline and you can merge conflicts. Leaderless when availability and write latency matter more than strict ordering and you have a conflict rule such as version vectors.

glossary.full: Shoot The Other Node In The Head
glossary.note: Fencing by force: the cluster powers off or disconnects a suspect node so it cannot keep writing.

sources.title: Martin Kleppmann, "How to do distributed locking" (2016)
sources.supports: the GC-pause scenario in which an expired lease leads to two writers; fencing tokens as increasing numbers checked by the storage (33 rejected after 34); zxid or znode version as a token; the storage must take an active role

sources.title: etcd documentation, "etcd3 API" (Lease API)
sources.supports: leases detect client liveness; keys attached to a lease are deleted when it expires or is revoked; TTL in seconds; refreshed through LeaseKeepAlive

sources.title: etcd client v3 concurrency package documentation
sources.supports: Election with Campaign, Proclaim, Resign, Leader and Observe; only one session can lead at a time; session TTL defaults to 60 seconds

sources.title: Apache ZooKeeper documentation, "ZooKeeper Recipes and Solutions" (Leader Election)
sources.supports: ephemeral sequential znodes under an election path; the smallest sequence number is the leader; each client watches the next-lower znode to avoid the herd effect

sources.title: Apache ZooKeeper documentation, "ZooKeeper Programmer's Guide" (Ephemeral Nodes, Sessions)
sources.supports: ephemeral znodes are deleted when the session ends; session timeout must be between 2 and 20 times tickTime; expiration is decided by the cluster, not the client

sources.title: Apache ZooKeeper documentation, "ZooKeeper Administrator's Guide" (tickTime, minSessionTimeout, maxSessionTimeout)
sources.supports: tickTime=2000 in the minimum configuration; minSessionTimeout defaults to 2 × tickTime and maxSessionTimeout to 20 × tickTime

sources.title: Kubernetes client-go, package leaderelection
sources.supports: "This implementation does not guarantee that only one client is acting as a leader (a.k.a. fencing)"; tolerant to clock skew but not to clock skew rate; 60 s lease with 30 s renew deadline tolerates a 2× faster clock

sources.title: Apache Hadoop, "HDFS High Availability Using the Quorum Journal Manager"
sources.supports: JournalNodes allow only a single NameNode to be a writer at a time; sshfence and shell fencing methods remain recommended to stop stale reads

sources.title: Mike Burrows, "The Chubby lock service for loosely-coupled distributed systems", OSDI 2006
sources.supports: sequencers carrying the lock generation number, validated by servers; lock-delay of up to one minute for servers that do not support sequencers

sources.title: ClusterLabs, Pacemaker Explained, "Fencing"
sources.supports: fencing makes an unresponsive node unable to run resources; also known as STONITH, Shoot The Other Node In The Head; power cut-off and fabric fencing

sources.title: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, ch. 5 "Replication" and ch. 8 "The Trouble with Distributed Systems" (O'Reilly, 2017)
sources.supports: single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication compared; process pauses and leases
